title: Web browsers
blurb: Chrome, Edge, Safari and Firefox: slow, crashing, pop-ups, certificate warnings.

remedies.title: Browser is slow or uses lots of memory
remedies.why: Dozens of open tabs, heavy extensions, or a single misbehaving page can slow the browser and the whole computer.

steps.text: Close tabs you don't need. Chrome and Edge show what each tab uses in their own Task Manager (Shift+Esc).
Turn off extensions you don't use: Chrome › ⋮ › Extensions, Edge › … › Extensions, Safari › Settings › Extensions, Firefox › ☰ › Add-ons.
Turn on memory saving: Chrome › Settings › Performance › Memory Saver; Edge › Settings › System and performance › Efficiency mode.
Update the browser: Chrome/Edge › Help › About; Safari updates with macOS; Firefox › Help › About Firefox.
Restart the browser; it reopens your tabs on most settings.

remedies.title: Browser crashes, freezes or shows "Aw, Snap!"
remedies.why: A broken extension, a damaged profile, hardware acceleration with an old graphics driver, or security software injecting into the browser.

steps.text: Reload the page. If only one site crashes, try it in a private window.
Turn off all extensions, then turn them back on one at a time to find the culprit.
Turn off hardware acceleration: Chrome/Edge › Settings › System › "Use graphics acceleration when available", then restart the browser.
Update the graphics driver through Windows Update › Advanced options › Optional updates, or the maker's site.
Make a new browser profile and see if the crashes stop; if they do, the old profile is damaged.
Check the computer's memory if many programs crash, not just the browser.

remedies.escalate: Note the error name (for example STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION) and whether other browsers crash too.

remedies.title: "Your connection is not private" or certificate warning
remedies.why: Usually the computer's clock is wrong, the network (hotel, airport) wants you to sign in first, or the site's certificate really is broken. Sometimes it's an attack.

steps.text: Check the date and time; fix them if they're off.
Check the date and time are set automatically.
On public Wi-Fi, open any plain site (like neverssl.com) to bring up the sign-in page, then try again.
Try the site from your phone on mobile data. If it warns there too, the site's certificate is broken: don't type passwords or card details.
Never click through a warning on your bank, email or work sites.

remedies.escalate: If it happens on many sites on your work network, tell IT at once (it can mean traffic is being intercepted).

remedies.title: Browser has a strange homepage, search engine or pop-ups
remedies.why: An unwanted extension or program changed the settings, or a site was allowed to send notifications.

steps.text: Remove extensions you didn't install or don't recognise.
Block site notifications: Chrome/Edge › Settings › Privacy › Site settings › Notifications, remove sites you don't know. Safari › Settings › Websites › Notifications.
Reset the browser: Chrome › Settings › Reset settings; Edge › Settings › Reset settings; Firefox › Help › More troubleshooting information › Refresh Firefox.
Uninstall programs you don't recognise that appeared recently (sort by install date).
Look in Applications for apps you don't recognise and move them to the Bin; check Login Items too.
Run a full virus scan.

remedies.escalate: On a work computer, report it to IT before entering any passwords.

remedies.title: A site looks broken or shows old content
remedies.why: The browser keeps copies of pages and cookies; a stale copy can break a site after it changes.

steps.text: Hard-reload the page: Ctrl+Shift+R on Windows, ⌘+Shift+R on Mac.
Clear that one site's data: click the icon left of the address › Cookies and site data (Chrome/Edge) or Safari › Settings › Privacy › Manage Website Data.
Clear everything cached: Ctrl+Shift+Delete (Chrome, Edge, Firefox) › Cached images and files. You'll stay signed in if you leave cookies unticked.

remedies.title: Website keeps asking me to sign in, or sign-in loops
remedies.why: The site's sign-in cookies are blocked or damaged, or a privacy extension removes them.

steps.text: Clear cookies for that site only and sign in again.
Allow cookies for the site (Chrome/Edge › Settings › Privacy › Third-party cookies › Sites allowed). Work sign-ins (Microsoft, Google) need them.
Try a private window, or turn off privacy and ad-block extensions for the site.
Check the computer's date and time.
Check the computer's date and time.

remedies.title: Download blocked or "file may be dangerous"
remedies.why: The browser or Windows SmartScreen thinks the file is risky, it comes over an insecure connection, or security software stopped it.

steps.text: Only keep a file you expected from a site you trust. If unsure, delete it.
In Chrome/Edge open Downloads (Ctrl+J) and choose Keep only if you trust it.
If Windows Security quarantined it and you're sure it's safe, check Protection history.
Get the file from the maker's own website instead of a download site.

remedies.escalate: Work computers often block downloads on purpose; ask IT for the program instead.

remedies.title: Links open in the wrong browser
remedies.why: Another browser is set as the default.

steps.text: Settings › Apps › Default apps › pick your browser › Set default.
System Settings › Desktop & Dock › Default web browser.
Outlook and Teams may open links in Edge on purpose; change that in Outlook › Settings › General › Files and browser links.

remedies.title: Browser stopped saving or filling passwords
remedies.why: Password saving was turned off, you're in a different browser profile, or sync is off.

steps.text: Check you're in the right profile (the picture at the top right).
Turn on saving: Chrome › Settings › Autofill › Google Password Manager › Settings; Edge › Settings › Profiles › Passwords; Safari › Settings › AutoFill.
Turn sync on so passwords come back on other devices.
On a Mac, passwords saved in Safari live in the Passwords app.

remedies.title: Website can't use my camera or microphone
remedies.why: The site was blocked, the browser itself isn't allowed by the system, or another app holds the camera.

steps.text: Click the icon left of the address bar › allow Camera and Microphone, then reload.
Allow the browser: Settings › Privacy & security › Camera (and Microphone) › let desktop apps access.
Allow the browser: Privacy & Security › Camera and Microphone › turn on your browser, then quit and reopen it.
Close Teams, Zoom and other apps that might be using the camera.

remedies.title: Web page prints blank, cut off or tiny
remedies.why: Pages built for screens don't always print well; scale, margins and background graphics settings matter.

steps.text: In the print dialog (Ctrl+P / ⌘P) open More settings: set Scale to Fit, margins Default, and tick Background graphics if parts are missing.
Choose Save as PDF first, check it looks right, then print the PDF.
Try printing from another browser.

remedies.title: PDFs open in the browser instead of my PDF app
remedies.why: The browser is set to show PDFs itself, or the browser is the default app for PDF files.

steps.text: Chrome › Settings › Privacy › Site settings › PDF documents › Download PDFs. Edge › Settings › Cookies and site permissions › PDF documents › Always download.
Set your PDF app as the default for .pdf: Settings › Apps › Default apps › search ".pdf".
Right-click a PDF › Get Info › Open with › choose the app › Change All.
